==Problem==
Aaliyah rolls two standard 6-sided dice. She notices that the product of the two numbers rolled is a multiple of <imath>6</imath>. Which of the following integers cannot be the sum of the two numbers?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 5\qquad\textbf{(B) } 6\qquad\textbf{(C) } 7\qquad\textbf{(D) } 8\qquad\textbf{(E) } 9</imath>

==Solution 1==

First, figure out all pairs of numbers whose product is 6. Then, using the process of elimination, we can find the following: 

<imath>\textbf{(A)}</imath> is possible: <imath>2\times 3</imath> 

<imath>\textbf{(C)}</imath> is possible: <imath>1\times 6</imath> 

<imath>\textbf{(D)}</imath> is possible: <imath>2\times 6</imath> 

The only integer that cannot be the sum is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 6}</imath>.

We can prove that B is correct because the only ordered pairs that add to 6 is <imath>(1,5)</imath> , <imath>(5,1)</imath>, <imath>(2,4)</imath>, <imath>(4,2)</imath>, and ,<imath>(3,3)</imath>, and these multiply to 5, 8, and 9.

Slight changes ~ VersatileGopher38

==Solution 2==

First, see that in order for the two numbers to have a product of 6, it must either have 6 as a factor or have factors that have a product of 6 (Notably <imath>2\times 3</imath>).

When we look at the answer choices, we see that answers <imath>C, D, E</imath> all are more than 6, so they can all be added as a sum of 6. Answer <imath>A</imath> works because <imath>2+3=5</imath>, so 6 is the only answer choice that doesn't work. Thus, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B) } 6}</imath>.
